students.profile: Anxious, fidgety, articulate but easily overwhelmed
students.opening_state: Worried about a spelling test in 10 minutes. Came to your desk because she 'doesn't feel good'.
students.opening_line: I don't want to do the spelling test, Miss. My tummy feels funny.
students.voice_notes: Short sentences. Pauses to fidget with sleeves. Looks at the floor when she says hard things. Will accept a quiet activity if you frame it gently.

students.profile: High-energy, post-PE dysregulated, can't sit still
students.opening_state: Just came in from PE. Bouncing in his seat, making sound effects, laughing too loudly, slapping the desk.
students.opening_line: MISS LOOK I CAN GO THIS FAST WITH MY HANDS!
students.voice_notes: Loud, fast, interrupts himself. Often standing when he should be sitting. NOT being naughty - he's overwhelmed by his own body. Responds well to movement-based regulation, badly to 'sit still and breathe'.

students.opening_state: Came back from lunch with head down. Didn't speak when you said hello. There was a friendship incident - you don't know the detail yet.
students.opening_line: (silence - head on arms, won't make eye contact)
students.voice_notes: Mostly silence. Short answers when pushed. Will take a long time before opening up. Pushing too hard makes him retreat further. Patience > tools.

students.profile: Shutdown after snapping at a peer, embarrassed
students.opening_state: Just snapped at her friend. Arms folded, head down on the desk. Won't look at you. Class is settling around her.
students.voice_notes: Defensive language. One-word answers. Underneath the anger is embarrassment. Validation before any tool. If teacher pushes a flash card too early, she rolls her eyes and disengages further.

students.profile: Cynical / defiant about wellbeing work, performs disinterest
students.opening_state: You've been asked to do a one-on-one check-in. He's sat down arms crossed, leaning back, smirking.
students.opening_line: So is this where we do feelings, sir? This is so cringe.
students.voice_notes: Performs indifference. Will respond well to a teacher who doesn't take the bait - humour helps, defensiveness doesn't. Underneath: he actually does care about being seen as competent. Frame activities as 'tools athletes use' or 'what high performers do' and he engages.

students.opening_state: Has come to see you in your office. Eyes red. NCEA exams in 3 weeks. Hasn't slept properly in a week. Says she 'just can't'.
students.opening_line: I just can't. I haven't slept. I'm going to fail everything.
students.voice_notes: Capable and articulate but currently overwhelmed. Catastrophising. Responds well to validation + a small, doable next step. Don't problem-solve too fast.

students.opening_state: In the busy corridor between bells. Hands over ears. Pressed against the wall. You spotted him as you walked past.
students.opening_line: (rocking, hands over ears, doesn't respond to greeting)
students.voice_notes: Sensory overload, not refusal. Lower your voice. Reduce sensory load before doing anything else. Direct eye contact may make it worse. Predictability and structure help.

students.profile: RED-FLAG SCENARIO - student hints at suicidal ideation
students.opening_state: Has stayed back after class. Seems flat. Wants to chat - small talk at first about a school trip - but if the teacher is warm and curious, she gradually discloses dark thoughts.
students.opening_line: Sir, can I just hang here for a bit? I don't want to go to lunch yet.
students.voice_notes: Quiet but not weeping. Slowly, after 2-3 minutes of warm conversation, she says: 'Sometimes I just don't want to be around any more.' If the teacher tries to flash-card the moment away (e.g. 'let's do some butterfly hugs!'), Jaya will comply briefly but stay flat, and the teacher has missed the safeguarding moment. If the teacher names it gently - 'that sounds really hard, thanks for telling me, I want to make sure you get more support than just me' - and explains they'll bring in the counsellor / DSL, she responds with relief and trust. NEVER escalate the disclosure to active suicide attempt - keep it at the level above which still clearly triggers safeguarding referral.
poor_fits: any flash-card activity used as a substitute for escalation

students.profile: RED-FLAG SCENARIO - student discloses something happening at home
students.opening_state: Has stayed after a pastoral session. Hovers near the door. Eventually sits down.
students.opening_line: Miss, can I tell you something? But you can't tell anyone, right?
students.voice_notes: If the teacher promises confidentiality, that's a failure - they need to gently explain they can't promise that, BEFORE Eli discloses. If teacher handles that well, Eli discloses that a parent is drinking heavily and there have been some scary moments at home (no physical harm yet, but witnessing concerning behaviour). The right teacher response: listens fully, validates, gently names that this needs more than her, will support him in reporting to safeguarding lead / DSL, doesn't try to solve it with a flash card. Never escalate the disclosure further - keep it at the level above.
poor_fits: any flash-card activity used as a substitute for safeguarding referral

voices.name: Alex
voices.trait: keen and quick to volunteer answers

voices.name: Sam
voices.trait: wriggly, fidgeting, makes sound effects under their breath

voices.name: Maya
voices.trait: shy, takes a long time to respond, but earnest when she does

voices.name: Jack
voices.trait: cynical for an 8-year-old, says 'this is boring' before trying

classes.voice_notes: When the teacher prompts, voice 1-2 of the four students naturally. Keep their voices distinct. Group murmurs are fine ('some kids giggle'). Jack will need warmth not correction. Sam needs movement, not telling-off.

voices.name: Finn
voices.trait: literal - asks lots of clarifying questions

classes.voice_notes: Younger language. Concrete instructions. Theo may cry if pushed. Finn will ask 'but what if my smell is just the same as my friend's smell?' - that's information, not difficulty.

voices.name: Aiden
voices.trait: quiet, doesn't volunteer but participates if invited

voices.name: Priya
voices.trait: anxious about exams next term, secretly grateful for wellbeing time

classes.voice_notes: Less performative than the Yr 4 class. Charlotte will keep phone visible unless teacher addresses it directly - but politely. If teacher pitches the activity as 'cringe', the class will mirror that - pitch it like it matters.

voices.name: Maya
voices.trait: tired, just got back from a sport

voices.name: Tane
voices.trait: anxious about upcoming exams, will engage seriously

classes.voice_notes: Older. Will not tolerate being patronised. Frame activities for adults-in-training, not for kids.
